meta.comment: Interactive hotspots. (u,v) are NORMALISED poster coordinates: 0..1 from the TOP-LEFT corner of poster.jpg. They drive both the AR anchors (mapped onto the tracked image plane) and the on-screen Demo Mode. The values below target the LANDSCAPE MSc poster (26SS-K12438440 …Buoyant_Jet_Flow). Each point sits on a real poster section; tweak (u,v) to line a dot up with your printed copy. Optional 'labelDir' (down|up|left|right, default down) sets which side the text label sits so neighbouring labels do not overlap.

hotspots.label: Test case & mesh
hotspots.body: A closed water tank (about 7.5 cm tall) at 293 K with a small warm jet entering at mid-height. The warm jet is lighter than the surrounding water, so buoyancy lifts it and a vertical thermal layer builds under the ceiling. A structured mesh of 1 mm cubic cells (~85,625) keeps the rCFD cell-to-cell shift maps clean; with Re ≈ 100 the jet is laminar (Fluent 2022 R2, Windows 11).

subs.label: Is the flow laminar or turbulent?

hotspots.label: rCFD workflow
hotspots.body: Recurrence CFD runs the expensive flow solve once and records the recurring cell-to-cell (C2C) shift patterns. The cheap replay loop then repeats to transport temperature — with no Navier–Stokes solve during replay. That is the source of the ~263× speed-up.

hotspots.label: Heat loss applied
hotspots.body: The top surface is allowed to lose heat, q = h(T − T∞). The physical value for water to still air is gentle (h ≈ 8 W/m²K), so a stronger h = 100 is used as the reference case to make the cooling easy to see. On the CFD side it is a Fluent source on the energy equation; on the rCFD side the same Newton cooling is applied to the transported scalar, both booked in the energy balance.

subs.label: How does wall heat loss change things?
Why does rCFD under-predict the cooling?

hotspots.label: Key discovery · ~31%
hotspots.body: The reused adiabatic database captures only about a third of the real heat loss. At the reference case h = 100 the rCFD replay cools by 3.03 K against the full CFD's 9.79 K (a ratio of ≈ 0.31), both read at t = 600 s. So roughly two-thirds of the cooling is missing. (At the gentle physical h = 8 the gap is wider still, 0.36 K vs 1.45 K ≈ 0.25, but the cooling there is hard to see.)
